verdicts.reason: No kill rule applies, because the mechanism ships. Storage OEMs build MRAM journals in-house: IBM has used Everspin MRAM in FlashCore since 2018 and FCM5 carries a few hundred MB. The card overstates margin and understates TRL and the incumbent list.

verdicts.reason: No kill rule applies. Every component exists: UCIe/AIB die-to-die IP and LPDDR5X controller/PHY IP are commercial, NVIDIA Grace proves 512-bit LPDDR5X at ~546 GB/s, and the minimum path (~$50-90M [ESTIMATE]) is T3, far below $1B. The headline bandwidth is wrong. 4-8 x64 LPDDR5X-8533 packages give 0.27-0.55 TB/s (68.3 GB/s each, computed), not 0.5-1 TB/s. 1 TB/s needs ~15 packages or LPDDR6, which is under half an HBM3E stack (~1.2 TB/s) but 4-14x its capacity. A winning axis remains: capacity and bandwidth per dollar without HBM allocation, plus moving the memory PHY off expensive leading-edge die area. But the named buyers already attach LPDDR directly with licensed IP (Qualcomm AI200, d-Matrix Corsair [UNVERIFIED-T]), and Amkor Arizona is anchor-customer-only, so packaging is offshore.

verdicts.reason: The core value claim has no evidence. The card says DoD HPCMP centers and NNSA labs will pay a premium for CXL expanders because they carry U.S.-fabbed Manassas DDR4. C-70 was killed for this same claim (batch_10, R1). The canonical landscape finds no U.S.-origin memory premium: TAA treats Korean, Taiwanese and Japanese DRAM as compliant, COTS is BAA-exempt, and memory pays 0% under Section 232 (01_LANDSCAPE 0 item 7, 7.3). The card's buyer evidence is misread. The Everspin $40M deal is an Amentum subcontract to stand up on-shore Toggle-MRAM process capability, not a premium on COTS DRAM. The provenance is thin too. Micron's back-end hubs are Malaysia and India, the controller is TSMC-made, Manassas output goes first to Micron's auto Strategic Customer Agreements (logged snippets), and SMART/Penguin already ships DDR4 behind CXL. Bandwidth-bound HPC nodes are the worst fit for a DDR4-over-CXL tier.

Logged snippets (A2, mram-info): a $40M, 2.5-year subcontract with Amentum for Toggle-MRAM process tech and foundry services. DoD pays for capability, not for U.S.-origin COTS DRAM in HPC.

verdicts.reason: The only independent product of this kind is gone. Enfabrica's ACF-S/EMFASYS used CXL controllers to pool up to 18 TB behind an Ethernet SuperNIC, and NVIDIA took it in 2025-09 for a reported >$900M in cash and stock, hiring the CEO and staff and licensing the technology (Blocks & Files, StorageNewsletter, via search snippet). For the named buyer (hyperscalers and GPU clouds), a new custom ASIC wins no axis. Commodity RDMA NICs, open-source Mooncake Transfer Engine/NIXL and CXL-backed memory servers already deliver GPU-reachable capacity per dollar (the card's own evidence, productized as C-45). NVIDIA owns the silicon version and bundles it with ConnectX/BlueField and Dynamo. An entrant spends a T3 (~$50M+) program and 4+ years just to reach parity. None of the card's three sources shows the silicon mechanism; all are software.
